26553-turandot-the-chinese-sphinx:
Sabilla Novello freely translated this verse play from Schiller and published it in London in 1872, pricing it at one shilling. It is called a dramatic oddity on its title page, and its scene is Peking and its environs. The cast lists Altoum, Khan of the Celestial Empire, his ministers Pantaloon and Tartaglia, and the princess Turandot, heiress to the throne.

Turandot, known as the Chinese Sphinx, exacts a cruel death from suitors who fail her trial, and heads on poles above the town gate show the price. Into Peking comes Kalaf, Prince of Tartary, long thought dead, with his old tutor Barak. Adelma, a captive princess, watches him with feeling. The play mixes comedy, disguise, and menace around a suitor who risks his life for the princess.
79598-the-sky-jinx:
Raoul F. Whitfield wrote this tale of the air. Its hero is Eddie Bride, a flyer who had won a name in France as a man of hard luck. Now he seems out for a new mark of the same kind with the air watch of the Philippine Isles. The tale is told by a man who trusts the eye for a face. His mate, Prop Owens, is the reverse: weak on faces, but a wonder at the sound of a voice.

The scene is the old Walled City in the dry time of year. Heat lies on Manila when no wind comes in from the bay. All is so dry that it cracks, and a man feels a worn taste in his mouth. The folk of the land grin at the heat and bear it.
